nameStory: The rhomboid fingernailclam gets its name from its diamond-shaped (rhomboid) shell that's about the size of a fingernail. Like other fingernailclams, you could theoretically use the tiny shell as a miniature fingernail, though it would be quite the conversation starter! The scientific name Sphaerium means 'little sphere,' referring to the rounded, ball-like shape when the shell is closed.
description: The rhomboid fingernailclam is a tiny freshwater bivalve that lives in the sandy and muddy bottoms of New England's ponds, streams, and lakes. These diminutive clams are typically less than half an inch long, with a distinctive diamond-shaped shell when viewed from the side. Unlike their marine cousins, these little clams spend their entire lives in fresh water, filtering microscopic particles from the water column. Their shells are usually yellowish-brown to gray, and they're often discovered by accident when sifting through sediment or examining aquatic plants.

idTips.label: Diamond-shaped shell
idTips.description: The shell has a distinctive rhomboid (diamond-like) outline when viewed from the side, wider in the middle and tapering at both ends, feeling smooth and slightly glossy to the touch

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Shell measures less than half an inch long, small enough to sit comfortably on your fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Yellowish-brown coloration
idTips.description: Shell ranges from pale yellow to brownish-gray, often with a slightly translucent quality that lets light shine through the thinner areas

idTips.label: Smooth shell texture
idTips.description: Shell surface feels smooth when rubbed gently with your finger, lacking the prominent ridges or grooves found on related species

idTips.label: Freshwater habitat
idTips.description: Found only in freshwater environments, never in brackish or salt water, usually buried in soft sediment that feels silty between your fingers

habitat: Rhomboid fingernailclams live in the soft, muddy or sandy bottoms of slow-moving streams, ponds, and lakes throughout New England. They prefer areas with fine sediment where they can easily burrow, often in shallow water near the edges of water bodies where organic matter accumulates. You'll typically find them in association with aquatic vegetation and other small freshwater invertebrates in areas with minimal water flow.

seasonality.spring: Active period begins as water temperatures rise, with clams moving closer to the surface in sediment. This is often the easiest time to spot them as they're more active in filtering and may be visible at the sediment surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're actively feeding and reproducing. Look for them in the top inch of sediment in shallow, warm areas of ponds and slow streams.
seasonality.fall: Clams begin burrowing deeper into sediment as temperatures drop. Still findable but require more digging through the soft bottom substrate.
seasonality.winter: Deeply buried in sediment, essentially dormant. Very difficult to locate as they may be several inches down in the mud, waiting for spring's return.

funFact: These tiny clams are hermaphrodites that can actually brood their babies in a special pouch, releasing fully-formed miniature clams rather than helpless larvae - it's like having a built-in nursery that produces clam babies ready to start their own independent lives!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other fingernailclams in the same genus, but the rhomboid's distinctive diamond shape sets it apart from the more oval grooved fingernailclam and the ribbed striated fingernailclam. Remember: rhomboid equals diamond-shaped, like the diamond suit in a deck of cards.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'fingernailclam,' these aren't closely related to marine clams you might eat - they're in their own specialized family adapted for freshwater life. The extremely low observation count (only 6 recorded in New England) doesn't necessarily mean they're rare, but rather that they're easily overlooked due to their tiny size and sediment-dwelling lifestyle.
compareHints: The rhomboid fingernailclam's diamond-shaped outline distinguishes it from its relatives: the grooved fingernailclam has prominent concentric ridges and a more oval shape, while the striated fingernailclam shows distinct radiating lines from the shell's peak. The rhomboid's smooth shell surface and wider-in-the-middle profile make it the most geometrically distinct of the New England fingernailclams.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its fingernailclam relatives, the grooved species stands out for its pronounced concentric ridges, while the rhomboid fingernailclam is more diamond-shaped and the striated species has finer, more closely-spaced lines.

Herrington fingernailclam is more circular than its relatives - the Grooved fingernailclam has distinct ridges you can feel, the Rhomboid is diamond-shaped, and the Striated has obvious parallel lines across the shell.
The Striated Fingernailclam differs from the Grooved Fingernailclam by having finer, more numerous ridges across its shell surface.
